prompt: In the CAP theorem, what does C mean?
hint: Not the C of ACID.

choices.text: A transaction leaves the database obeying its constraints
choices.why: That is ACID's consistency.

choices.text: Every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy
choices.why: Right: linearizability.

choices.text: Every node runs the same version of the software
choices.why: Versions have nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The data is backed up consistently every night
choices.why: Backups are not what the theorem is about.

prompt: Stated precisely, what does the theorem say a node must do during a partition?
hint: Refuse, or answer and risk...

choices.text: Shut down until the partition ends
choices.why: Shutting down is one way of refusing, not the only choice.

choices.text: Elect a new leader on each side
choices.why: That is one algorithm's behaviour, not the theorem.

choices.text: Refuse what it cannot answer correctly, or answer and risk being wrong
choices.why: Right: give up A, or give up C.

choices.text: Keep both consistency and availability by waiting longer
choices.why: Waiting for ever is refusing.

prompt: Match each letter of CAP to what it means in the theorem.
hint: The table of the first section.

pairs.right: every read sees the most recent write
every request to a live node gets a non-error answer
the system works when messages between nodes are lost

prompt: Why can a distributed system not choose to give up P?
hint: Is a partition a feature or an event?

choices.text: Because P is the cheapest of the three to provide
choices.why: Cost is not the argument.

choices.text: Partitions happen to it whatever it chooses
choices.why: Right. The only choice is what it does when one happens.

choices.text: Because the theorem's proof assumes it and nothing else
choices.why: The point is about networks, not proofs.

choices.text: It can, by running all nodes in one data centre
choices.why: One data centre still has switches, pauses and overloaded nodes.

prompt: A node stops answering for eight seconds during a garbage-collection pause and then carries on. What did the other nodes experience?
hint: Can they tell a slow peer from a broken network?

choices.text: Nothing unusual; a pause is not a failure
choices.why: To them it was silence, exactly as a partition looks.

choices.text: A crash, which they can tell apart from a partition
choices.why: They cannot tell any of them apart until a timeout.

choices.text: A partition, as far as they could tell
choices.why: Right. Silence looks the same whatever its cause.

choices.text: A network error message from the paused node
choices.why: A paused node sends nothing at all.

prompt: What does a "CA" system actually describe?
hint: How many machines?

choices.text: A cluster that never has network problems
choices.why: No cluster can promise that.

choices.text: A single machine with no peers
choices.why: Right, such as one PostgreSQL server.

choices.text: A system that is consistent and available during partitions
choices.why: That is what the theorem rules out.

choices.text: A cloud database sold with a high availability guarantee
choices.why: A guarantee in a contract is not a CAP property.

prompt: What did the standby answer when asked to run an UPDATE?
hint: One copy decides.

choices.text: It updated its copy and passed the change to the primary
choices.why: A standby never takes writes.

choices.text: It updated its copy only, so the two diverged
choices.why: The standby refused.

choices.text: An error: a read-only transaction
choices.why: Right. It accepts reads and refuses writes.

choices.text: It forwarded the UPDATE to the primary automatically
choices.why: PostgreSQL does not forward writes from a standby.

prompt: How does the lab's standby keep its copy up to date?
hint: Look at `pg_stat_replication` and the standby's command.

choices.text: It copies the whole database with `pg_basebackup` every minute
choices.why: `pg_basebackup` runs once, at the start.

choices.text: It streams and replays the primary's write-ahead log
choices.why: Right, after one initial copy.

choices.text: The application writes every change to both servers
choices.why: The application writes only to the primary.

choices.text: Both servers share one volume on disk
choices.why: Each has its own volume, `primary` and `standby`.

prompt: With synchronous replication and the standby disconnected, what happened to the UPDATE?
hint: Look at `wait_event`.

choices.text: It waited on `SyncRep`, and the client gave up
choices.why: Right. The primary would not finish a write it could not copy.

choices.text: It failed at once with an error saying the standby was gone
choices.why: There was no error; there was a wait.

choices.text: It succeeded on the primary and was visible to other sessions
choices.why: Other sessions still saw 12.

choices.text: It was applied on the standby only
choices.why: The standby was unreachable and refuses writes anyway.

prompt: What exit code did `timeout 5` report when it killed the waiting client?
hint: The line after the update.

prompt: The client gave up after five seconds. When the network came back, both servers showed 11. What is the lesson?
hint: What did the client believe, and what was true?

choices.text: The update was lost, as the client assumed
choices.why: Both servers show the update applied.

choices.text: The standby applied the change on its own initiative
choices.why: The primary finished the waiting transaction.

choices.text: Synchronous replication loses writes during a partition
choices.why: It did not lose this one; it delayed it.

choices.text: The sale succeeded though the client thought it failed; a retry needs an idempotency key
choices.why: Right. Lesson 2's uncertain outcome, again.

prompt: In PostgreSQL, the standbys that must confirm a commit are named by the setting ___.
hint: It starts with `synchronous_standby`, and the lab set it to `'*'`.

prompt: During the partition with asynchronous replication, what did a read from the standby return?
hint: The primary said 10.

choices.text: An error, because the standby could not reach the primary
choices.why: The standby kept answering reads.

choices.text: 11, a value that was no longer true
choices.why: Right: available, and stale.

choices.text: 10, because it asked the primary first
choices.why: It cannot reach the primary during the partition.

choices.text: Nothing until the network came back
choices.why: It answered at once.

prompt: The primary is destroyed while asynchronous replication is two seconds behind, and the standby is promoted. What is lost?
hint: What had the primary acknowledged and not yet streamed?

choices.text: Nothing, because the standby replays everything on promotion
choices.why: It can only replay what it received.

choices.text: Only uncommitted transactions
choices.why: Committed ones from the last two seconds are lost too.

choices.text: The whole database since the last backup
choices.why: The standby has everything up to the lag.

choices.text: Writes clients were told were committed, in the last two seconds
choices.why: Right: up to the replication lag.

prompt: Match each situation to how synchronous replication behaves.
hint: The left column of the table.

pairs.left: a read from the standby during a partition
pairs.right: the same value as the primary
nothing a client was told is lost

prompt: What does the "else" in PACELC add to CAP?
hint: When there is no partition...

choices.text: A third choice during partitions
choices.why: The else is about the time without a partition.

choices.text: Without a partition, the trade is latency or consistency
choices.why: Right, and it is made on every request.

choices.text: Partitions can be prevented with enough engineering
choices.why: PACELC assumes they happen.

choices.text: Latency is irrelevant when the network works
choices.why: The lab measured the opposite.

prompt: Why were 500 commits slower with synchronous replication when nothing was broken?
hint: What does each commit wait for?

choices.text: The primary writes each change twice to its own disk
choices.why: The extra wait is for the standby.

choices.text: Synchronous mode turns off PostgreSQL's caching
choices.why: Caching is unchanged.

choices.text: Each commit waits for the standby's confirmation
choices.why: Right: a round trip per commit, every day.

choices.text: The standby was overloaded by the benchmark
choices.why: It only replayed the changes; the wait was the round trip.

prompt: Where do etcd and ZooKeeper sit, and why?
hint: What failure do they exist to prevent?

choices.text: Availability in both halves, to stay fast
choices.why: They choose consistency on purpose.

choices.text: Latency without partitions, availability with them
choices.why: That is the Cassandra-style corner.

choices.text: They do not replicate, so CAP does not apply
choices.why: They replicate to a majority on every write.

choices.text: Consistency in both halves: two leaders at once is the failure they prevent
choices.why: Right.

prompt: The lab's PostgreSQL was CP and then AP within ten minutes. What misreading does that refute?
hint: A property of the product?

choices.text: That CAP applies only to NoSQL databases
choices.why: It refutes a different idea, about products.

choices.text: That CP or AP is a property of the product
choices.why: Right. It is a property of how it is configured and used.

choices.text: That partitions are rare
choices.why: Partitions being rare is true; the lab did not test it.

choices.text: That replication is slower than a single server
choices.why: That is PACELC's point, not a misreading.

prompt: A single PostgreSQL server enforces a foreign key on every transaction. Is it "consistent" in CAP's sense, ACID's sense, or both?
hint: With one copy, every read sees the latest write.

choices.text: Only ACID: CAP's consistency needs several replicas
choices.why: One copy trivially returns the latest write.

choices.text: Only CAP: foreign keys are not part of ACID
choices.why: Constraints are exactly ACID's consistency.

choices.text: Both, but for different reasons
choices.why: Right: its constraints hold, and with one copy every read is the latest.

choices.text: Neither, until a standby is added
choices.why: A standby adds a way to be CAP-inconsistent, not the other way round.

prompt: With N = 5 replicas and W = 3, what is the smallest R that guarantees every read overlaps every write?
hint: R + W > N.

prompt: N = 3, W = 1, R = 1. What does that setting give up?
hint: Is R + W > N?

choices.text: Availability: any replica down stops everything
choices.why: One replica is enough for each request.

choices.text: Latency: every request waits for all three
choices.why: Each request waits for one.

choices.text: The guarantee that a read sees the latest write
choices.why: Right. 1 + 1 is not greater than 3.

choices.text: Durability: the write is never stored
choices.why: It is stored on at least one replica.

prompt: With N = 3, W = 3 and R = 1, what happens to writes when one replica is down?
hint: How many must acknowledge?

choices.text: They succeed on the other two
choices.why: Three acknowledgements are required.

choices.text: They fail
choices.why: Right: fast reads, paid for with fragile writes.

choices.text: They are stored and read back from the missing replica later
choices.why: The missing replica cannot store anything.

choices.text: They turn into reads automatically
choices.why: Writes do not change kind.

prompt: Which of Quitanda's operations does the lesson put on the consistency side?
hint: A wrong answer here costs money.

choices.text: Showing the catalogue's photos
choices.why: Yesterday's photo costs little.

choices.text: Showing "12 left" on the product page
choices.why: An approximate number is fine there.

choices.text: Keeping a customer's basket
choices.why: A basket that briefly shows a removed item is a small cost.

choices.text: Taking units out of stock at checkout
choices.why: Right. Two customers buying the last bag is the mistake to avoid.

prompt: Why does the lesson say "refuse" often costs less than it sounds, for a payment?
hint: Who notices each mistake, and when?

choices.text: Refused payments are retried automatically by the bank
choices.why: The customer retries, not the bank.

choices.text: Refusing is free in every cloud provider's pricing
choices.why: Pricing is not the argument.

choices.text: A visible failure is retried now; a double charge is found weeks later
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Customers prefer errors to slow pages
choices.why: The comparison is between an error and a wrong charge.

prompt: Put the lab's synchronous-replication experiment in order.
hint: Set, cut, write, look, heal.
items: Disconnect the standby from the network

prompt: Quitanda's two stores share the stock of coffee through two database nodes, one in each store, linked over the internet. The link fails on a Saturday morning. What must the design have decided in advance?
hint: Each store can still sell; can each still be right?

choices.text: Nothing; replication will catch up when the link is back
choices.why: Both stores may sell the last bag meanwhile.

choices.text: Which store's clock is authoritative
choices.why: Clocks do not decide who may sell.

choices.text: Whether each store keeps selling and accepts overselling, or stops selling coffee during the cut
choices.why: Right: availability or consistency, decided per operation.

choices.text: How many retries to allow per sale
choices.why: Retries do not cross a broken link.
